item.title: Foundational Mechanics, Approximation Theory, and Bio-inspired Sensing
item.description:
This thrust develops foundational mechanics-aware representations, approximation methods, and sensing concepts that support structural health monitoring and digital twin development.

The aim is to create new mathematical and mechanical tools for representing structural response, damage fields, stiffness changes, and sensing mechanisms in ways that are useful for diagnosis and prediction.

Mechanics-aware approximation of structural response fields

This direction studies how displacement, strain, curvature, stiffness, and damage-related fields can be represented using continuous and adaptive approximation functions.

item.title: Openings
item.description:
I am actively looking for motivated PhD and M.Tech students interested in mechanics-informed AI, structural health monitoring, digital twins, scientific machine learning, computer vision, sensing technologies, and AI-assisted infrastructure monitoring.

PhD students are expected to pursue long-term research directions, while M.Tech students can take up focused thesis problems with clear research objectives and potential for strong technical contributions. Motivated B.Tech students interested in early research exposure are also encouraged to connect.

item.title: Uncertainty-aware SHM and Bayesian Inference
item.description:
This thrust develops uncertainty-aware methods for structural health monitoring, damage diagnosis, model updating, and decision support.

The goal is to move from deterministic monitoring outputs toward confidence-aware interpretation, where engineers can understand not only what the model predicts, but also how uncertain or reliable that prediction is.

Uncertainty-aware structural diagnosis

This direction studies how uncertainty in measurements, models, environmental conditions, and structural parameters affects damage detection and condition assessment.

Suitable for: PhD / M.Tech

item.title: Scientific Machine Learning and Equation Discovery
item.description:
This thrust develops scientific machine learning methods for discovering interpretable models of structural and dynamical systems from data.

The emphasis is on combining data-driven learning with mechanics, governing equations, physical constraints, and reduced-order representations so that machine learning models remain meaningful for engineering analysis.

Physics-guided model discovery for structural systems

This direction investigates how measured or simulated structural response data can be used to discover interpretable models that are consistent with mechanics.

item.title: System Identification and Digital Twin Updating
item.description:
This thrust develops methods to identify structural properties, reconstruct hidden states, track evolving behaviour, and update computational models using monitoring data.

The long-term objective is to support digital twins that are not only visual representations, but mechanics-aware models that can evolve with measurements from real structures.

State estimation for structural dynamic systems

This direction develops methods to estimate structural states such as displacement, velocity, acceleration, modal response, and other hidden quantities from noisy or incomplete measurements.

item.title: Damage Detection, Localization, and Condition Assessment
item.description:
This thrust develops mechanics-informed methods for detecting, localizing, and interpreting damage in civil infrastructure.

The goal is to move beyond black-box classification and develop damage diagnosis methods that are connected to structural response, deformation patterns, stiffness changes, wave propagation, and mechanics-based interpretation.

Mechanics-guided damage indicators

This direction develops response-based indicators that can reveal stiffness loss, localized deterioration, or abnormal structural behaviour using displacement, strain, curvature, vibration, or energy-based information.

Suitable for: PhD / M.Tech / Research Interns

item.title: About
item.description:
Prof. Ashish Pal is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Civil Engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay. His research lies at the intersection of structural engineering, scientific computing, sensing technologies, and artificial intelligence.

His work focuses on developing mechanics-informed intelligent systems for structural health monitoring, digital twins, scientific machine learning, and resilient infrastructure monitoring.

Research Vision
#

The long-term goal of the research is to develop intelligent infrastructure systems capable of autonomous sensing, interpretation, prediction, and decision support through the integration of mechanics, sensing technologies, data, and machine intelligence.

item.title: Physics-guided Sensing and Signal Processing for SHM
item.description:
This thrust develops physics-guided sensing, signal-processing, and computer-vision methods for structural health monitoring. The focus is on extracting reliable structural response from noisy, incomplete, multi-rate, and heterogeneous measurements.

The broader goal is to convert raw measurements from cameras, accelerometers, strain sensors, drones, and other sensing systems into physically meaningful information about structural behaviour.

Noise-robust structural response reconstruction

This direction develops methods to reconstruct displacement, velocity, acceleration, curvature, and other response quantities from noisy structural measurements.
